findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the failure-disposition contract for the trim arm: any lookup or call exception is caught and treated as a non-fatal no-op (returns False, logged at most once), never surfacing to the tool caller or daemon, and the gauge release always completes.
evidence: "Where the C library has no `malloc_trim` (macOS, musl) it is a no-op returning `False`."
No statement on exceptions raised by the lookup or the call within the releaser.
findings.finding: The plan adds a new failure arm inside `InFlightGauge._releaser`, the shared release path for every certified call, daemon, boot sweep and idle tick. It states a disposition only for 'malloc_trim absent' (no-op returning False). It does not state the disposition when the ctypes library load or symbol lookup raises (for example OSError, or TypeError from loading a NULL library), or when the trim call raises. In particular it does not say whether the exception is swallowed so the release still completes and the caller never sees it, or whether it propagates out of `track`/`admit` exit into the tool response or the daemon thread.
findings.location: Approach / Scope (`_malloc_trim()` cached ctypes lookup; `_releaser` calls it)
scenarios: The libc lookup raises on a platform where the C library cannot be loaded by name. Every certified tool call then fails on exit with an unrelated exception, even though its work succeeded.
findings.suggested_fix: Add: 'release_freed_heap() never raises: any exception from the ctypes lookup or malloc_trim is caught, cached as unavailable, and returns False; the releaser decrements before calling it, so release always completes.' Add a unit test that monkeypatches the lookup to raise and asserts the certified call still returns normally.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Define release_freed_heap()'s return value (e.g. True when glibc malloc_trim was found and called, regardless of its result), and change the test to say 'True when malloc_trim resolves (glibc), False otherwise' instead of 'True on Linux'.

findings.finding: The test expects release_freed_heap() to 'return True on Linux and False elsewhere', but the plan never says what True means. glibc's malloc_trim returns 1 only if it actually gave memory back to the OS and 0 otherwise. If the function passes that value through, the Linux assertion depends on the heap's state and can flake. The plan also says musl has no malloc_trim and returns False, yet musl is Linux, so 'True on Linux' contradicts its own no-op rule.
findings.location: Testing — '`release_freed_heap()` returns `True` on Linux and `False` elsewhere'; Approach — 'Where the C library has no `malloc_trim` (macOS, musl) it is a no-op returning `False`'
scenarios: CI on ubuntu-latest runs the test when there is nothing to trim. If the glibc return value is passed through, the function returns False and the test fails even though the code is correct.
findings.suggested_fix: Return `True` whenever the cached `ctypes` lookup found `malloc_trim` and it was called, ignoring glibc's 0/1 result. Gate the assertion on whether the symbol resolved (glibc), not on `sys.platform == 'linux'`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Say whether the trim on the zero transition is meant to cover memory still referenced when the release runs (the tool return value and partial args in _CountedHandoff.run/_thread_offloaded). Either accept and document that the next zero transition (idle-sync tick) picks it up, or move or repeat the trim to after the result is dropped, and extend the Linux test to have the counted call return a large value.
evidence: _CountedHandoff.run: `try: return self._call() finally: self._release()` — the release happens before the return value leaves the worker frame
_thread_offloaded: `call = functools.partial(fn, *args, **kwargs)` holds the call arguments until the coroutine finishes, after the release
start_idle_sync returns None when there is no tracker dir, so the periodic tick that would trim later is not guaranteed
findings.finding: The plan assumes that when the gauge reaches zero, the gate's memory has already been freed. In the code, the release runs before the tool's return value and call arguments are dropped. _CountedHandoff.run calls self._release() in its `finally` while the result of self._call() is still live, and `functools.partial(fn, *args, **kwargs)` still holds the arguments. The same is true of the _sync_wrapper/track path. That result is handed to AnyIO and serialized on the event loop afterwards, so anything allocated in the worker's arena for it is freed after the trim. Those pages are only returned at the next zero transition, which may be the next idle-sync tick or may never come if no store exists.
findings.location: Approach — 'When a release takes the count to zero, call a new release_freed_heap()'; src/rebar/_mcp_health.py _CountedHandoff.run (lines 245-253), _thread_offloaded (286-293)
scenarios: A certified tool returns a large result (e.g. a long review payload) and the gauge reaches zero in the worker's finally. The trim runs while that payload is still referenced, and its pages stay in the arena once AnyIO drops it.
A deployment with no ticket store has no idle-sync loop, so nothing else brings the gauge back to zero and the memory released after the first trim stays held.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in Approach how memory freed after the zero-crossing (handoff return values, cyclic garbage) gets trimmed: either name the 120 s idle-sync tick as the backstop or make the trim run after the late frees (for example, a deferred trim or a gc pass first).
evidence: _CountedHandoff.run: `try: return self._call() finally: self._release()`. The release, and so the trim, runs before the return value leaves the worker.
run_idle_sync_loop takes gauge.hold() and releases every IDLE_SYNC_INTERVAL_S = 120.0, so the count reaches zero again on every idle tick, but start_idle_sync returns None when there is no store.
The plan's Linux test drops all strings inside the counted region, so it cannot catch memory freed after the release.
findings.finding: The trim fires synchronously at the instant the count reaches zero, before some of the work's memory is freed. _CountedHandoff.run calls self._release() in its finally while the tool's return value is still alive and not yet serialized or sent. Memory held in reference cycles (exception tracebacks, frames) is freed only when the cyclic GC runs, which can lag behind an idle process. Pages freed after the zero edge are trimmed only at the next zero crossing. In production that is the next 120 s idle-sync tick, but the plan never names that tick as the backstop, and no store means no tick.
findings.location: Approach ('When a release takes the count to zero, call a new release_freed_heap()'); src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:245-253 (_CountedHandoff.run), :437-449 (idle-sync hold)
scenarios: The last gate's large prompt or result strings sit in a reference cycle and are freed by a later GC pass; nothing trims again until another counted op or idle tick.
A server running without a store (no idle-sync thread) keeps memory freed after the last zero crossing indefinitely.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the thread the trim runs on (e.g. off the event loop via a worker thread or a single-flight background trigger), and state the expected cost when there is little to free plus whether a debounce or minimum interval applies.
evidence: "When a release takes the count to zero, call a new `release_freed_heap()` that invokes glibc `malloc_trim(0)` ... outside the gauge lock"
"`malloc_trim(0)` brings it to 24 MB in 70 ms"
The gauge counts "each idle-sync tick (line 437)", so the trim fires on every tick.
findings.finding: The plan does not say which thread executes malloc_trim, or bound its cost and frequency. The trim runs synchronously in _releaser on whatever thread releases the last hold. For async `track`/`admit` releases this can be the event-loop thread, and the plan's own measurement is 70 ms per ~1 GB trimmed. It also fires on every 0-transition: every idle-sync tick and every lone certified call. There is no debounce, so lightly loaded servers repeatedly release and refault pages. A request admitted while the trim runs also contends on arena locks.
findings.location: Approach ("call a new `release_freed_heap()` ... outside the gauge lock")
scenarios: A certified call finishes on the event loop after a gate. A 70+ ms trim blocks all other in-flight async handlers.
Steady trickle traffic triggers a trim after every request, adding latency and page-fault churn.
findings.suggested_fix: Run release_freed_heap() via a single-flight background thread (skip if a trim is already running) rather than inline in _releaser when called from an async context. Note in the plan that trims with little free memory cost <1 ms, so per-tick trimming is acceptable.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State which thread executes the trim and whether it is on the tool-response path; specify how a trim racing a fresh admit or a repeated zero transition is handled (accept, debounce, or hand off to a background thread).
evidence: "`_releaser` calls it when the count reaches zero"
"outside the gauge lock"
"each idle-sync tick (line 437)"
findings.finding: The trim is a side effect run synchronously by whichever thread performs the release that reaches zero. That thread may be a certified tool call's thread on its exit path, a daemon, or an idle-sync tick. The plan does not say whether this adds the trim's cost (70 ms measured on about 1 GB, possibly more on a fragmented heap) to the last caller's response. Because the trim runs after the gauge lock is dropped, a new admit can already be in flight. The 'trim when idle' condition is therefore check-then-act, and the trim walks arena locks concurrently with fresh allocations. Repeated zero transitions, such as each idle-sync tick or back-to-back calls, can also start overlapping or repeated trims with no debounce.
findings.location: Approach ("When a release takes the count to zero, call a new `release_freed_heap()` ... outside the gauge lock")
scenarios: A sequential client making certified calls pays a malloc_trim on every call's exit, because each call takes the gauge back to zero.
An idle-sync tick releases to zero and starts a trim while a new certified call has just been admitted, so the trim contends with that call's allocations.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Extend the no-op contract to platforms where no C library can be loaded (Windows), guard the lookup so it never raises, and test the False path by simulating a failed or absent libc (monkeypatch) so it runs in Linux CI.
evidence: "Where the C library has no `malloc_trim` (macOS, musl) it is a no-op returning `False`."
"(Linux, CI `ubuntu-latest`)"
Platform fact: on Windows there is no 'libc' for ctypes to dlopen; a name or NULL-handle load fails rather than yielding a library missing the symbol.
findings.finding: The no-op fallback is defined only for C libraries that lack `malloc_trim` (macOS, musl). Windows, a supported platform, has no POSIX libc to load through ctypes, and the plan does not cover that case. The 'returns False elsewhere' test runs only in Linux CI (`ubuntu-latest`), so the non-Linux branch is never exercised. A Windows host running the MCP server or library could hit an exception from the libc lookup on every gauge release.
findings.location: Approach ("Where the C library has no `malloc_trim` (macOS, musl) it is a no-op") / Testing ("returns `True` on Linux and `False` elsewhere")
scenarios: Platform `Windows` (developer workstation running the MCP server): the first certified call's release triggers the libc lookup, which raises. The call surfaces an error, or the release path breaks, instead of performing the documented no-op.
findings.suggested_fix: Guard the lookup with `sys.platform.startswith('linux')` plus try/except (OSError, AttributeError, TypeError) returning None. Add a unit test that monkeypatches the lookup to fail and asserts `release_freed_heap()` returns False.
